overview: This file documents U.S. and Allied policymaking on the postwar iron and steel industries of Japan and, in its final papers, Manchuria. It begins with a State Department memorandum seeking flexibility over Japan’s permitted pig-iron capacity, then records Far Eastern Commission decisions on the temporary retention of electric furnaces and the removal as reparations of surplus steel-rolling capacity. Subsequent memoranda, draft directives, and SCAP acknowledgments trace how those policies were transmitted through the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee and Joint Chiefs of Staff to General Douglas MacArthur. The closing memoranda route and critically evaluate a report proposing iron and steel production in Manchuria, particularly questioning its costs, assumptions, and implied profitability.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on assured Japanese pig-iron capacity
subfiles.from: Mr. Martin and C. I. Hodge, JK
subfiles.about: The memorandum requests authority to accept an annual Japanese pig-iron capacity of up to 800,000 metric tons in Far Eastern Commission negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The approved U.S. position allowed an assured capacity of 500,000 metric tons, subject to negotiating adjustments, while the Pauley recommendation contemplated temporarily retaining 1.5 million tons until imported pig iron became available. SCAP likewise favored temporary retention of the higher capacity because imported ore and pig iron were not yet assured. Since the United Kingdom proposed 800,000 tons, received broad support, and argued that this level was needed to process economically mined Japanese ore, the authors recommend authority to accept that figure.

subfiles.title: Johnson letter transmitting the electric-furnace policy decision
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Secretary General, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.to: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Johnson transmits the Far Eastern Commission’s policy decision on temporary retention of electric steel furnaces for implementation as a directive to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Johnson explains the Commission’s authority to formulate occupation policy and the U.S. Government’s responsibility to prepare implementing directives. He reports unanimous approval of the electric-furnace decision at the Commission’s thirty-sixth meeting. The letter also requests secure transmission and delayed press release until forty-eight hours after receipt in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Certification of the electric-furnace decision
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Secretary General, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Johnson certifies that the attached electric-furnace policy decision is a true copy of the text adopted by the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: The certification records unanimous adoption at the Commission’s thirty-sixth meeting in Washington on December 6, 1946. It establishes the enclosed text as an authenticated copy of the original decision.

subfiles.title: Policy decision on temporary retention of electric steel furnaces
subfiles.from: Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: The decision permits Japan temporarily to retain additional electric steel-furnace and integrated rolling capacity because of the coal shortage.
subfiles.summary: In addition to the previously authorized 100,000 metric tons of annual capacity, Japan may retain up to 300,000 metric tons of additional electric-furnace capacity through June 30, 1947. SCAP may request a review if occupation needs require an extension. The facilities are still to be designated for eventual removal under the interim reparations program.

subfiles.title: Johnson letter transmitting the steel-rolling policy decision
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Secretary General, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.to: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Johnson transmits the Far Eastern Commission’s decision defining the steel-rolling capacity to be retained in Japan or removed as reparations.
subfiles.summary: The letter reports unanimous approval of the steel-rolling decision at the Commission’s thirty-sixth meeting. It asks the United States to prepare and transmit an appropriate directive to the Supreme Commander. As with the furnace decision, Johnson requests secure transmission and a press embargo lasting until forty-eight hours after receipt in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Certification of the steel-rolling decision
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, Secretary General, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Johnson certifies the enclosed steel-rolling policy as a true copy of the text unanimously adopted by the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: The certification identifies the decision as a product of the Commission’s thirty-sixth meeting on December 6, 1946. It authenticates the copy for official transmission and implementation.

subfiles.title: Policy decision on the Japanese steel-rolling industry
subfiles.from: Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: The decision makes Japanese steel-rolling capacity beyond that needed for 2,775,000 metric tons of annual balanced output immediately available as reparations.
subfiles.summary: The paper defines the steel-rolling industry as plants producing such basic shapes as rails, rods, bars, tubes, plates, strips, sheets, and structural shapes. It fixes Japan’s retained requirement at the capacity needed for a balanced annual output of 2.775 million metric tons. All excess rolling capacity is designated for immediate availability as reparations.

subfiles.title: Hilldring memorandum forwarding the electric-furnace draft directive
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hilldring asks SWNCC to forward the draft electric-furnace directive through the Joint Chiefs of Staff to General MacArthur.
subfiles.summary: The draft is based on the Far Eastern Commission’s unanimous policy decision and quotes that decision verbatim. Hilldring requests transmission to MacArthur and asks that any questions be referred back to the State Department. He also conveys the Commission’s requirements for acknowledgment, secure handling, and delayed public release.

subfiles.title: Draft directive on temporary retention of electric steel furnaces
subfiles.from: State, War, and Navy Departments
subfiles.to: General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: The draft directive implements the Commission policy temporarily retaining specified electric-furnace capacity in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The directive authorizes retention through June 30, 1947, of up to 300,000 metric tons of electric-furnace capacity beyond the previously authorized 100,000 tons, together with integrated rolling mills. MacArthur may seek review if occupation requirements justify an extension. Temporary retention is not to delay designation of the facilities for reparations removal.

subfiles.title: Hilldring memorandum forwarding the steel-rolling draft directive
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hilldring asks SWNCC to forward the steel-rolling draft directive to General MacArthur through the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the draft reproduces the Far Eastern Commission’s December 6 policy decision verbatim. It asks for transmission to MacArthur and State Department clarification of any questions raised by the Joint Chiefs. It also calls for acknowledgment, transmission security, and coordination of the public release in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Draft directive on the steel-rolling industry
subfiles.from: State, War, and Navy Departments
subfiles.to: General Douglas MacArthur, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: The draft directive orders that Japanese rolling capacity exceeding the requirement for 2.775 million metric tons of annual output be made available as reparations.
subfiles.summary: The directive defines the covered industry by its production of basic rolled, drawn, and extruded steel shapes. It adopts a balanced annual output of 2,775,000 metric tons as the basis for retained capacity. Capacity beyond that level is to become immediately available for reparations.

subfiles.title: SWNCC transmittal of SCAP acknowledgment on electric furnaces
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Chairman, State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: SWNCC forwards SCAP’s acknowledgment of the directive concerning temporary retention of electric steel furnaces.
subfiles.summary: At the Joint Chiefs of Staff’s request, Hilldring sends the enclosed SCAP message to the Department of State. The message is intended for further transmission to the Far Eastern Commission as confirmation that the directive reached Tokyo.

subfiles.title: SCAP telegram acknowledging the electric-furnace directive
subfiles.from: GHQ SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.to: War Department for the Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.about: SCAP reports receipt and internal distribution of the Far Eastern Commission decision on electric steel furnaces.
subfiles.summary: The restricted-priority message acknowledges the December 15 transmission concerning temporary retention of electric furnaces. It states that the interested SCAP staff section received the decision on December 16. The message was distributed to the Joint Chiefs and several senior military offices and commanders.

subfiles.title: Duplicate SWNCC transmittal memorandum on electric furnaces
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Chairman, State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: This copy repeats the SWNCC memorandum forwarding SCAP’s acknowledgment of the electric-furnace directive.
subfiles.summary: Marked as a copy accompanying the original, the memorandum again records the Joint Chiefs’ request that SCAP’s message be sent to the State Department. Its purpose is to support notification of the Far Eastern Commission that the directive had been received.

subfiles.title: Duplicate SCAP acknowledgment on electric furnaces
subfiles.from: GHQ SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.to: War Department for the Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.about: This restricted copy repeats SCAP’s acknowledgment that the electric-furnace decision reached the interested staff section.
subfiles.summary: The message identifies the earlier War Department radiogram and confirms staff receipt on December 16. It duplicates the acknowledgment enclosed with the SWNCC transmittal memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memorandum notifying the Commission of electric-furnace directive receipt
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hilldring asks the Secretary General to circulate SCAP’s acknowledgment of the electric-furnace directive to Commission members.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts that the directive was sent to General MacArthur on December 15. It quotes SCAP’s report that the decision reached the interested staff section on December 16. The Secretary General is requested to make this confirmation available to all members of the Commission.

subfiles.title: SWNCC transmittal of SCAP acknowledgment on steel rolling
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Chairman, State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: SWNCC forwards SCAP’s acknowledgment of the Far Eastern Commission directive on Japan’s steel-rolling industry.
subfiles.summary: At the request of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Hilldring transmits the enclosed secret message to the Department of State. Its intended use is to notify the Far Eastern Commission that the steel-rolling directive was received in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: SCAP telegram acknowledging the steel-rolling directive
subfiles.from: GHQ SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.about: SCAP reports receipt and staff distribution of the Far Eastern Commission decision on the steel-rolling industry.
subfiles.summary: The secret-priority message refers to the December 14 War Department transmission. It confirms that the interested staff section received the steel-rolling decision on December 16. Copies or information were routed to the Joint Chiefs and named senior military offices and admirals.

subfiles.title: Memorandum notifying the Commission of steel-rolling directive receipt
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hilldring asks the Secretary General to circulate SCAP’s acknowledgment of the steel-rolling directive.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the directive based on the December 6 policy decision was transmitted to General MacArthur on December 14. It quotes SCAP’s confirmation that the interested staff section received it on December 16. The acknowledgment is to be shared with members of the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum for the Manchurian iron and steel paper
subfiles.from: William McAfee, CA
subfiles.about: McAfee forwards the attached Manchurian iron and steel paper for information, evaluation, and comment at Ringwalt’s request.
subfiles.summary: The short routing note records Mr. Ringwalt’s request that the paper be sent to DRF. DRF is asked both to review the material and to provide an evaluation and comments.

subfiles.title: Critical evaluation of Bayne’s Manchurian iron and steel report
subfiles.from: C.R.B.
subfiles.about: The author questions the accuracy, technical basis, cost assumptions, and investment appeal of Bayne’s report on Manchurian iron and steel production.
subfiles.summary: C.R.B. states that a technical expert is needed to assess Bayne’s figures and expresses doubts about their accuracy. The report estimates hypothetical 1947 output and sales in Chinese National Currency but apparently lacks a credible schedule of capital and production costs. Its assumption that cheap scrap from North China and Manchuria could be converted into highly profitable finished products is dismissed as a speculative borrower’s pitch to a potential lender.

interest: The file is especially useful for reconstructing the bureaucratic chain by which Allied industrial-reparations policy moved from Far Eastern Commission decision to State Department draft, SWNCC and Joint Chiefs transmission, SCAP receipt, and formal notification back to the Commission. Its quantitative limits—500,000 or 800,000 tons of pig iron, 400,000 tons of temporarily retained electric-furnace capacity, and 2.775 million tons of rolled products—show how occupation authorities tried to reconcile demilitarization, reparations, coal shortages, domestic ore, and import availability. The duplicate transmittals, security markings, acknowledgment messages, and press-release instructions also illuminate the mechanics of interagency and occupation-era communications. The final Manchurian memorandum offers a contrasting contemporary view of Chinese industrial-development proposals and the skepticism with which American officials assessed their financial assumptions.
